# LUMEN: a physics-pretrained, conformally calibrated network for lunar soil mineralogy, chemistry and maturity — with a pre-registered head-to-head against three published methods

*Draft generated by `scripts/step09_paper.py` from the tables in `tables/` (2026-10-23). Every
number in it is filled from the same tables as `RESULTS.md`; the prose is hand-written.
Authors: D. Sheth et al. (to be completed).*

## Abstract

Methods that retrieve lunar mineralogy from reflectance spectra are rarely compared on
identical data. Their validation often lacks a zero-information baseline and an
out-of-distribution test. We present LUMEN, a hybrid physics + deep-learning method:

- a 1-D convolutional network pretrained on 400,000 spectra from a domain-randomised
  Hapke simulator (with physically modelled space weathering and no evaluation soil among its
  end-members);
- fine-tuned on real laboratory soils;
- with a deep-ensemble, conformal uncertainty;
- and an identifiability gate that withholds targets without demonstrable skill.

**Evaluation.** On the 19 Lunar Soil Characterization Consortium soils (75 spectra), under a
pre-registered leave-one-soil-out and leave-one-mission-out protocol, we compared LUMEN with
the published methods of Korokhin et al. (2024), Jung et al. (2026) and Fernández-Díaz et al.
(2026), and with classic baselines.

**Results (leave-one-soil-out).**

- LUMEN predicts FeO to 1.26 wt %, TiO₂ to 0.70 wt % and the
  seven-part modal composition to 2.66 vol % (mean absolute error over soils).
- It reduces the error of Korokhin et al.'s mineral proportions by
  54–74 % on every mineral, significant after
  correction.
- It meets all of Jung et al.'s accuracy claims on their test soils, where their method
  misses the ilmenite claim.
- Its FeO error is 42 % lower than our re-implementation of Fernández-Díaz et
  al.'s pipeline.
- **Against a random forest on the same inputs, its advantage is significant only for
  maturity.**

**Orbital data.** On real M³ spectra at 18 returned-sample landing sites, the
lab-trained network does **not** transfer:

- with no site training its FeO error is 6.4 wt %, worse than predicting the
  mean of the other sites;
- even after recalibration (3.6) it trails Fernández-Díaz's pipeline and a
  band ratio (3.1 and 3.2), though no method explains much
  of the variance.
- Fine-tuning on the other landing sites' M³ spectra fixes this: FeO error
  2.6 wt % (R² 0.46), the best of all methods, though with 18 sites the
  margin is mostly not significant.

**Ablations and uncertainty.**

- Pretraining helps.
- Two of the planned ingredients — SSA-space mixup and synthetic replay — did not improve on
  pretraining plus real-data fine-tuning.
- Leave-one-mission-out errors are roughly 1.9× larger.
- Olivine is not identifiable from these spectra.
- Conformal intervals reach nominal coverage under leave-one-soil-out and fall slightly short
  out of distribution.

We release the code, the pre-registration, and every intermediate table.

## 1. Introduction

Mapping lunar mineralogy, chemistry and maturity from orbital reflectance spectra underpins
studies of the Moon's crustal evolution, volcanism and space weathering. Two families of
methods dominate.

- **Physics-based inversions.** These include Hapke radiative transfer with Bayesian sampling
  (Jung et al., 2026) and Shkuratov-model fitting by Nelder–Mead or by a neural network trained
  on synthetic spectra (Korokhin et al., 2024). They are interpretable, but non-unique and
  sensitive to the end-member set and to the optical-constant model.
- **Empirical regressions.** These relate spectral features to sample chemistry, for example
  wavelet features compressed by an autoencoder and fed to a random forest for FeO
  (Fernández-Díaz et al., 2026). They are accurate in-sample, but are trained on a few dozen
  ground-truth sites and rarely tested out of distribution.

Our independent reproductions of these three methods expose four common gaps:

- **(G1) a sim-to-real gap.** Physics-only inversions are mis-calibrated on real soils. On the
  19 LSCC soils, Korokhin's fits lose to a mean-of-other-soils baseline for olivine. Jung's
  worst-case ilmenite error (17.6 points) exceeds the claimed bound (10), and the prior alone
  meets two of their three accuracy claims.
- **(G2) untested identifiability.** Korokhin's network recovers orthopyroxene, olivine and the
  grey absorber with R² ≤ 0.32 on its own synthetic test set, yet these are mapped.
- **(G3) no calibrated uncertainty.** Jung's released sampler degenerates to 0–1 % unique
  particles, so its credible intervals are not posteriors.
- **(G4) weak validation.** Fernández-Díaz's 50 FeO samples sit on about 15 distinct coordinates
  and the headline MAE is a 5-sample hold-out. No study compares against a zero-information
  baseline.

We propose LUMEN, a hybrid that keeps the physics where it helps (pretraining and physically
consistent augmentation) and lets real soils correct it. It addresses each gap:

- **G1:** a domain-randomised Hapke simulator for pretraining, then fine-tuning on real soils
  with a new physically exact augmentation (SSA-space mixup);
- **G3:** a deep ensemble with conformal calibration;
- **G2:** an identifiability gate that withholds targets without demonstrable skill;
- **G4:** a pre-registered evaluation under leave-one-soil-out and leave-one-mission-out, with
  paired tests against all three methods on identical data and a zero-information baseline.

We report where LUMEN does not win as prominently as where it does.


## 2. Data

**Laboratory spectra and ground truth.** We use the Lunar Soil Characterization Consortium
(LSCC) suite: 9 mare soils (Taylor et al., 2001) and 10 highland soils (Taylor et al.,
2010).

- Each soil was sieved into <10, 10–20, 20–45 and <45 µm fractions and measured at RELAB
  (i = 30°, e = 0°).
- The 70181 10–20 µm spectrum is absent, which leaves 75 spectra.
- Ground truth:
  - modal mineralogy (point counts, vol %) for the three finer fractions (56 spectra), merged
    into seven parts: plagioclase (PLG), low-Ca pyroxene (LCP = orthopyroxene + pigeonite),
    high-Ca pyroxene (HCP), olivine (OLV), ilmenite (ILM), agglutinitic glass (AGG), and other
    (volcanic glass, K-phases, other);
  - bulk FeO, TiO₂, Al₂O₃, CaO and MgO;
  - the ferromagnetic-resonance maturity index Is/FeO for all 75 spectra.
- Every spectrum is convolved to the 71 Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M³) global-mode bands
  between 540.8 and 2497.1 nm, with Gaussian responses of FWHM equal to the band spacing.

**End-member library.** We use 49 RELAB spectra of lunar mineral separates and glasses (17
plagioclase, 7 low-Ca and 11 high-Ca pyroxene, 6 olivine, 4 ilmenite, 2 volcanic and 2
synthetic lunar glasses).

- They come from mare basalts, highland rocks, a non-LSCC soil (62241) and synthetic glasses.
- No end-member derives from any of the 19 evaluation soils. Every RELAB agglutinate separate
  comes from an LSCC soil, so agglutinates are modelled physically.

**M³ scenes.**

- The Shapley-region strip M3G20090728T214215 analysed by Korokhin et al. (2024), lines
  13918–14805.
- An Apollo 16 block, M3G20090607T110414.
- The two Aristarchus ROI blocks of Jung et al. (2026).

All are L2 reflectance.

## 3. Method

### 3.1 Physics simulator

- **Grain optics.** Each end-member's imaginary index k(λ) is obtained by inverting the Hapke
  (1993) equivalent-slab model at the separate's nominal grain size.
  - R(k) is non-monotonic: it falls to an opacity floor, then rises as surface reflection grows
    with k. The root is therefore bracketed on the physical, falling branch.
  - This removes the k = 1 clamping we found for a dark synthetic glass. Every end-member now
    reproduces its own reflectance to < 1e-10.
- **Space weathering.** Nanophase iron adds α = 36π z(λ) φ / λ (Hapke 2001; Lucey & Riner
  2011). Microphase iron is a grey absorber. Agglutinates are a glass host (a mix of a
  feldspathic and a mafic synthetic glass) loaded with npFe0 and mpFe0.
- **Synthetic soils.** Each synthetic soil draws:
  - a petrological regime (feldspathic / basaltic / broad Dirichlet priors on the crystalline
    proportions, truncated at ≤ 20 % ilmenite and ≤ 60 % olivine of the crystalline part);
  - a maturity that sets the agglutinate fraction and the npFe0 loads;
  - grain sizes from 4 to 150 µm;
  - one end-member per phase;
  - a calibration tilt, ±7 % scale and 0.2–0.8 % noise.
- **Mixing and labels.**
  - Components mix intimately in single-scattering albedo with cross-section weights vol/D.
  - Chemistry labels follow from stoichiometry: nominal phase chemistry with a molar Fe ↔ Mg
    exchange jitter, and the agglutinate carrying the bulk composition of the non-agglutinate
    part.
  - Is/FeO = 2270 · npFe0 / FeO sets only the scale of the pretraining target.
- **Set size.** We generate 400,000 spectra.

### 3.2 Network

- **Input.** Two channels × 71 bands: log reflectance and convex-hull continuum-removed
  reflectance, each standardised per band with *synthetic* statistics. No real-data statistic
  enters the input.
- **Body.** Five 1-D convolutions with GroupNorm and GELU, two max-pools, and a 256 → 128
  trunk (0.36 M parameters).
- **Heads.**
  - A Dirichlet head (concentrations α) for the 7-part composition. Its loss is the Dirichlet
    NLL plus an L1 term on the mean, whose weight was fixed on synthetic data.
  - Heteroscedastic Gaussian heads trained with β-NLL (β = 0.5; Seitzer et al., 2022) for the
    five oxides and log₁₀(Is/FeO).
  - Auxiliary grain-size and npFe0 heads, used during pretraining only.

### 3.3 Training

- **Pretraining.** Five ensemble members are pretrained on the synthetic set (15 epochs,
  AdamW, one-cycle).
- **Fine-tuning.** Each member is fine-tuned per fold for 1500 steps. Each step draws:
  - 16 real training spectra;
  - 32 **SSA-mixups**: 2–3 training spectra, mixed in single-scattering albedo with
    cross-section weights from their nominal fraction sizes, with labels mixed exactly
    (composition by volume, chemistry by mass, Is/FeO weighted by mass × FeO);
  - 16 synthetic replay spectra.

  Real and mixed spectra receive the simulator's calibration / noise randomisation.
- **Pre-registration.** The schedule was pre-registered and never tuned on held-out data.

### 3.4 Uncertainty and identifiability

- **Ensemble moments.** The mean of the member means. The variance is the mean of the member
  variances plus the variance of the member means.
- **Conformal intervals.** Normalised scores |y − μ|/σ from the out-of-fold predictions of
  the other soils (or missions) give conformal half-widths q·σ. This is a CV+-style
  construction; the calibration residuals come from fold models that included the test soil.
- **Identifiability gate.** A target's leave-one-soil-out skill, 1 − MAE / MAE(fraction-matched
  mean of the other soils), carries a bootstrap CI. Only targets whose CI excludes zero are
  mapped.

## 4. Evaluation protocol

- **Splits.** Leave-one-soil-out (19 folds) and leave-one-mission-out (6 folds: A11, A12, A14,
  A15, A16, A17).
  - Every fraction of the held-out soil or mission is excluded from fine-tuning, mixup and
    inner model selection.
  - Leave-one-mission-out is the out-of-distribution test: holding out A16 removes every
    feldspathic soil, and holding out A17 every high-Ti soil.
- **Metrics.** Per-soil MAE (each soil's labelled fractions averaged, then the 19 soils
  averaged). Paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over soils, Holm-corrected over the 13 targets.
- **Baselines** (same folds, hyperparameters by inner group CV on training soils):
  - the fraction-matched mean of the other soils (zero-information reference);
  - PLS, ridge and random forest on the same features;
  - a random forest on raw reflectance;
  - the full Fernández-Díaz et al. (2026) pipeline re-implemented on the same spectra:
    db4 A2 + D2 wavelets, a 6-D autoencoder trained on M³ pixels or on synthetic spectra, and
    four regressors with their search grids; plus its no-autoencoder variant.
- **Comparisons with Korokhin et al. (2024) and Jung et al. (2026).** These use the published
  methods' own outputs on the same soils, from independent reproductions, scored exactly as
  each paper scores itself.
- **Ablations.** Zero-shot (synthetic only), real-only from scratch, scratch + mixup,
  pretrain + real, pretrain + mixup, and the full model. All are reported.


## 5. Results

### 5.1 Simulator

All self-tests pass.

- **k round trip.** Every end-member's k(λ) reproduces its measured reflectance to
  7.8e-11. Before the falling-branch fix, 13 bands of the synthetic L19
  glass were clamped at k = 1.
- **Prior.** Truncating the composition prior lowers the 99th-percentile synthetic TiO₂ from
  30.5 to 14.0 wt % (the LSCC maximum is 10.7) and
  FeO from 31.8 to 24.4 wt %.
- **Label model.** Modal composition × class-average phase chemistry reproduces the LSCC
  bulk oxides with r = 0.93–0.98. It is biased for mare TiO₂
  (+2.9 wt %), which affects only the scale of the pretraining labels.
- **Coverage of the real data.** The 75 LSCC spectra lie inside the synthetic cloud: their
  median nearest-neighbour distance is 0.102, against 0.144 between
  synthetic spectra.
- **Sim-to-real gap.** A classifier still separates real from synthetic spectra
  (AUC 0.97; 0.99 against noise-free synthetic spectra). On average, real
  soils are redder than their nearest synthetic neighbours.
- **Mixing test.** The measured <45 µm spectra are reproduced by linear mixtures of their
  sieve fractions to 0.6 % RMS. The bulk chemistry, however, could not
  discriminate between the mixing rules (Section 6).

### 5.2 Accuracy on the LSCC soils

Table 1 gives per-soil MAEs for the main methods; every method and target is in `RESULTS.md`.

**Leave-one-soil-out.**

- Against the fraction-matched mean of the other soils, the primary model (A4) has skill
  0.50 for composition and 0.72 for FeO.
- Against each classic baseline separately, A4 has the lower error on 12/13
  targets; the exception is olivine every time. Holm-corrected,
  it is significantly better than PLS on 9 targets and than the mean of the
  other soils on 10.
- **Against the strongest baseline, a random forest on the same features, only maturity is
  significant after correction** (FeO: raw p = 0.005, Holm 0.064).

**Leave-one-mission-out.**

- Every method degrades. A4's composition MAE rises from 2.66 to
  4.70 vol %, and its FeO MAE from 1.26 to 2.59 wt %.
- A4 remains lower than the random forest on 10/13 targets, but loses on
  olivine, "other" and MgO.
- For agglutinate and "other", A4 is not significantly better than the mean of the other
  soils, and for "other" no method has a lower error than that zero-information baseline.

### 5.3 Ablations

**The pre-registered primary model is not the best configuration** (Table 2).

- Pretraining on the synthetic set helps: A2 beats real-only training from scratch
  (A1) on 13/13 targets under leave-one-soil-out.
- The two other ingredients — SSA-mixup and synthetic replay — did not help:
  - adding them to the pretrained model (A4) lowered the error on only
    1/13 targets relative to A2;
  - none of the A4–A2 differences is significant after Holm correction.
- Mixup does help a model trained from scratch under leave-one-soil-out (A1m vs A1, lower on
  12/13), but not under leave-one-mission-out (2/13). It
  partly substitutes for pretraining rather than adding to it.
- The zero-shot model (A0), the physics-only analogue of Korokhin's network, has a
  composition MAE of 9.1 vol %, far above every fine-tuned model. This is the
  sim-to-real gap made concrete.

### 5.4 Head-to-head with the three published methods

**Korokhin et al. (2024).** Table 3 scores each method on the 5-mineral proportions, exactly
as their reproduction scores itself.

- Under leave-one-soil-out, A4 reduces the error for every mineral (Holm-significant on
  CPX, OPX, OLV, PLG, ILM), e.g. olivine 1.91 vs 7.44 and plagioclase
  5.55 vs 12.08 percentage points.
- Under leave-one-mission-out, A4 is still lower on 4/5 but significant only for
  OLV, and it is slightly worse for plagioclase (12.64 vs
  12.08).
- **Caveat.** Their inversion never sees an LSCC soil, while A4 is fine-tuned on the others.
  The like-for-like physics-only comparison is the zero-shot A0. It beats their fit on
  3/5 minerals but is significant only for OLV.
- **Maturity.** LUMEN's Is/FeO ranks the 19 soils better than their nFe parameter: Spearman
  ρ = 0.72 / 0.81 / 0.96 vs 0.55 / 0.37 / 0.44 for the <10 / 10–20 / 20–45 µm fractions.

**Jung et al. (2026).** On their four test soils at 20–45 µm:

- A4's worst-case crystalline errors are 1.00 (olivine), 1.24 (ilmenite)
  and 7.95 (plagioclase) percentage points under leave-one-soil-out. All three of
  their accuracy claims are met; their converged inversion has 17.56 for ilmenite.
- With n = 4 this is weak evidence. The zero-shot A0 also meets every claim, while the mean
  of the other soils fails the ilmenite and plagioclase claims.
- **Maturity.** LUMEN's Is/FeO correlates with the measured value at r = 0.99
  across the four soils, against -0.00 for their I_sm.

**Fernández-Díaz et al. (2026).** Their full pipeline is re-implemented on the same spectra
and folds (Table 4).

- Under leave-one-soil-out, A4's FeO MAE is 1.26 wt %. The published
  configuration (M³-trained autoencoder → random forest) has 2.17 wt %; their
  best variant on our data, wavelets → SVR-RBF without the autoencoder, has
  1.91 wt %.
- A4 is lower than all twelve variants (raw p < 0.05 for each), but only 3/12
  comparisons survive Holm correction over the variants.
- Under leave-one-mission-out, A4 has 2.59 wt % against 3.48
  (published configuration) and 2.91 (best variant, p = 0.49).
- **The autoencoder's effect depends on the protocol.**
  - Under leave-one-soil-out it mostly loses information, as the original reproduction found:
    the M³-trained autoencoder is worse than the raw wavelet coefficients for
    4/4 regressors.
  - Under leave-one-mission-out it helps the two linear regressors, and is worse than the raw
    coefficients for 2/4.

### 5.5 Uncertainty and identifiability

**The raw ensemble is overconfident.**

- Mean empirical coverage is 0.59 / 0.82 / 0.89 under leave-one-soil-out and 0.33 / 0.55 / 0.64
  under leave-one-mission-out, for nominal 68 / 90 / 95 %.
- Conformal calibration with normalised residuals restores nominal coverage under
  leave-one-soil-out (0.68 / 0.90 / 0.95) and comes close under leave-one-mission-out
  (0.64 / 0.86 / 0.92).

**Exact CV+ confirms this.** Exact CV+ uses models that saw neither the calibration nor the
test soil (930 extra fine-tunes). Its coverage is 0.69 / 0.90 / 0.96 under leave-one-soil-out and
0.70 / 0.88 / 0.93 under leave-one-mission-out (normalised residuals), so the approximation was
slightly conservative out of distribution.

**The identifiability gate passes 11/13 targets.** It withholds olivine and the
"other" class: their skill confidence intervals include zero, and olivine's point estimate
is negative. Under leave-one-mission-out the agglutinate fraction's skill also loses
significance.

### 5.6 Application to M³

**Calibration.** On the Apollo 16 landing-site pixel, Korokhin's published lab-scale
calibration reproduces the LSCC 62231 spectrum to 9.1 % RMS, against
1.4 % for the re-derived line.

**Apollo 16 site.** LUMEN estimates FeO 5.0 wt %, against 4.9
measured for 62231 and 4.6 for the Apollo 16 mean. It overestimates TiO₂
(2.1 vs 0.6). Because 62231 is in the final training set, this is
a sanity check, not a validation.

**Shapley scene.** The maps of the 11 identifiable targets show the expected
mare/highland contrasts: FeO 10.2 vs 6.6 wt %, Al₂O₃ 20.0 vs
24.3 wt %. Fresh craters stand out as immature.

- Korokhin's high-Ca pyroxene map is anti-correlated with LUMEN's
  (r = -0.79), and theirs places more clinopyroxene in the highlands than in the
  mare.
- Their maturity parameter nFe and LUMEN's Is/FeO are nearly unrelated across the scene
  (r = -0.28).

**Aristarchus ROIs.**

- LUMEN finds much less olivine and much more plagioclase in the crystalline fraction than
  Jung's posteriors (plagioclase 52 % vs 29 % in ROI B).
- LUMEN's olivine output failed the identifiability gate, and the training soils contain
  little olivine. The disagreement is therefore a domain-shift warning rather than evidence
  against Jung.

### 5.7 Landing-site validation on M³ (pre-registered addendum)

**Setup.** M³ L2 spectra were fetched at all 18 distinct coordinates of
Fernández-Díaz et al.'s 50 returned samples (66 strips within 0.01°). Each site
is scored once, with its samples averaged.

**LUMEN does not transfer to orbital spectra.**

- Applied with the published lab-scale calibration and without any landing-site data — for
  Apollo sites, by models that never saw that mission's soils — LUMEN's FeO MAE is
  6.36 wt %.
- It is biased low by -5.7 wt % and is worse than predicting the mean of the
  other sites (3.70).
- It is significantly worse than 5 of 10 comparators after Holm
  correction.
- A leave-one-site-out linear recalibration of its output reduces the MAE to
  3.56. That is still behind:
  - the best Fernández-Díaz variant (FD-AE-M3/SVR-lin 3.07);
  - a two-band ratio (3.18).

**No method does well on this task.**

- Fernández-Díaz as published (autoencoder → random forest) reaches 3.48
  wt % (R² = 0.02).
- No method exceeds R² = 0.27 over the 18 sites.
- The ground truth is part of the difficulty: one Apollo 17 coordinate mixes samples
  spanning 7.0 wt % FeO.

### 5.8 Orbital fine-tuning (pre-registered addendum)

**Setup.** LUMEN is fine-tuned on the M³ pixel spectra of the other 17 sites (594
pixels; FeO only, mixed 1:1 with laboratory spectra) and evaluated leave-one-site-out.

**It becomes the most accurate method on M³.**

- FeO MAE 2.64 wt %, R² = 0.46.
- Comparators: 3.07 for the best Fernández-Díaz variant, 3.48
  for their published configuration, and 3.18 for the band ratio.
- It has a lower error than every comparator. With 18 sites, however, the differences are
  significant after Holm correction for only 2 of 10.



## 6. Discussion

**What carried the gains.**

- The decisive ingredient is the combination of physics-based pretraining with fine-tuning on
  real soils.
- Neither alone suffices:
  - the zero-shot network is the worst LUMEN variant, consistent with the sim-to-real gap the
    simulator analysis exposes (real spectra lie inside the synthetic distribution yet are
    separable from it);
  - training on real soils from scratch is worse than starting from the pretrained weights,
    on 13/13 targets under leave-one-soil-out (though on only
    7/13 out of distribution).
- This supports the premise behind design goal G1, that physics-only inversions are
  mis-calibrated, and suggests that the role of a simulator is to provide a good
  representation rather than a calibrated forward model.

**What did not help.**

- SSA-space mixup was meant to enlarge the 18-soil training set with physically consistent
  mixtures. It helps a network trained from scratch under leave-one-soil-out, but adds nothing
  once the network is pretrained, and synthetic replay does not help either.
- Two explanations are consistent with the data:
  - Pretraining already provides the smoothness over composition space that mixup was meant
    to supply.
  - The cross-section mixing weights are poorly constrained. Our own test (Section 5.1) shows
    that sieve-fraction spectra mix linearly, but the LSCC chemistry cannot pin down the mass
    proportions well enough to validate the weighting rule.
- We kept the full model as the pre-registered primary and report the simpler configuration's
  better numbers as an ablation, not as the result.

**Head-to-head, read carefully.**

- **Korokhin and Jung.** LUMEN's large margins over these two methods partly reflect what each
  method sees. Their physics inversions never see an LSCC soil; LUMEN is fine-tuned on the other
  soils. Two numbers matter here:
  - the like-for-like physics-only comparison: LUMEN's zero-shot model is better than
    Korokhin's fit on 3/5 minerals, but significantly so only for olivine;
  - Jung's test set is four soils, too few for strong conclusions.
- **Fernández-Díaz** is the fairest comparison: their pipeline was trained on exactly the same
  folds. LUMEN reduces the FeO error by 42 % against the published
  configuration. That pipeline is not much better than a random forest on raw reflectance,
  however, and against that random forest LUMEN's FeO gain does not survive multiple-testing
  correction.
- We consider the defensible claims to be:
  1. LUMEN is more accurate than all three published methods on identical data in
     19 of 20 head-to-head comparisons, the exception being
     PLG vs Korokhin (LOMO). Its margins over the two physics inversions are large and, under
     leave-one-soil-out, significant;
  2. under leave-one-soil-out, LUMEN's maturity estimate is significantly better than every
     classic baseline, and it ranks soils better than both physics methods' maturity
     parameters;
  3. its advantage over a well-tuned conventional regressor is real in magnitude (lower error
     on 12/13 targets) but not yet statistically established with 19 soils.

**Out of distribution.**

- Holding out a whole mission roughly 1.9-folds the error.
- Agglutinate and "other" glass lose their skill.
- These are the conditions of orbital mapping, where soils unlike any training sample are
  common. This is why the identifiability gate and conformal intervals matter. The gate
  withholds olivine (no skill even in leave-one-soil-out) and the "other" class, and the
  conformal intervals widen appropriately, though they fall slightly short of nominal coverage
  out of distribution.
- The Aristarchus comparison illustrates the risk. LUMEN finds little olivine where Jung et
  al.'s posterior finds abundant olivine, but LUMEN's olivine output is exactly the quantity
  the gate flags as unidentifiable.

**Laboratory-to-orbit transfer is the open problem.**

- The landing-site test shows that accuracy on laboratory spectra does not carry over to M³
  through one linear calibration. LUMEN underestimates FeO by 5.7 wt %
  on average and compresses the range.
- The lab advantage over the three papers is therefore a laboratory result.
- On orbital FeO, the methods trained directly on M³ landing-site spectra, including
  Fernández-Díaz's, do better.
- A small orbital training signal closes most of the gap. Fine-tuning on the other 17
  landing sites makes LUMEN the most accurate method on M³ (Section 5.8). More landing-site
  ground truth is the limiting resource.

## 7. Limitations

- **Small ground truth.** 19 soils, 75 spectra, and only 56 with modal mineralogy. All
  significance statements are over 19 soils; several numerically large improvements do not
  survive Holm correction.
- **Conformal intervals.** The headline intervals are CV+-style. Exact CV+ with pair-held-out
  models gives very similar coverage, so this approximation is not a material limitation.
- **Laboratory spectra, not orbital ones.** The M³ application relies on a single linear
  calibration to the laboratory scale.
  - The published calibration reproduces the Apollo 16 laboratory spectrum to 9.1 %,
    against 1.4 % for a re-derived line.
  - We applied no destriping, and stripes are visible in the maps.
  - The single landing-site check uses a soil that is also in the training set.
- **Simulator labels are biased.** The simulator's chemistry labels overestimate mare TiO₂ by
  2.9 wt %, and its maturity scale is set by a single constant. Both are
  re-learned during fine-tuning, but they limit the zero-shot model.
- **One schedule, not tuned.** The fine-tuning schedule was fixed a priori and not tuned. The
  ablations show that a simpler configuration would have done better.
- **Orbital ground truth is thin.** It has 18 sites, with coordinates as listed by
  Fernández-Díaz et al. (one mixes stations). The laboratory-trained model fails on it.

## 8. Conclusions

On laboratory spectra, physics-based pretraining followed by fine-tuning on real soils gives
a single network that:

- predicts lunar soil mineralogy, chemistry and maturity more accurately than three recently
  published methods, on identical data and under identical protocols;
- is accompanied by calibrated uncertainty and an explicit statement of which outputs are
  identifiable.

The comparison also shows how much of the published methods' error is removed simply by
honest calibration against real soils, and how little of LUMEN's own advantage over a strong
conventional regressor can yet be established with the 19 soils available.

On orbital M³ spectra the same model fails at the returned-sample landing sites. A useful
orbital product will need training signal from orbit, not only from the laboratory.

All code, the pre-registration (`METHOD_NOTES.md`, committed before any model was scored on
real data) and every table behind this draft are in the repository. `RESULTS.md` lists every
number, including those not shown here.
